    SpaceX (SPCX): the toll road is real. The price already assumes the vision.

    SpaceX sells room on a rocket that comes back, and earns more when it fills that room with Starlink. At the Oct 2 close the equity already assumes the vision path. Research only.

    SpaceX (SPCX): the toll road is real. The price already assumes the vision.

    Research only, not financial advice.

    SpaceX sells one scarce thing: room on a rocket that comes back. It can sell that room to a customer, or fill it with its own Starlink satellites and rent the connection for years. Think of a toll road whose owner also runs the largest truck fleet on it. The number to remember is 3.4x. One Falcon 9 sold to a customer brought in about $58M in the first half of 2026. The same rocket filled with Starlink earns about $195M of revenue over an assumed four-year satellite life, about 3.4 times as much. That is revenue, not cash, and the life is an assumption.

    Our research view at $158.96 is that the price already assumes the vision path, and under our stated assumptions we see more downside than upside over 12 months.

    What changed on Oct 4

    This note patches the Oct 4 v3 draft. It does not replace the mechanism work. Three things changed, and one did not.

    The price line was refreshed. Markets were closed on Oct 3 and Oct 4, so the latest regular-session close is still Friday, Oct 2. Two public pages, saved this evening, both show $158.96. StockAnalysis timestamps that close at 4:00 PM EDT. CNBC's saved page shows the same close and dates it 10/02/26 EDT. Their after-hours prints differ by one cent and are not used. No price file, price chart, or price feed was pulled.

    EDGAR was read first. The S-1, the 424B4 prospectus, and the 10-Q for the quarter ended June 30, 2026 were saved on Oct 4. Submissions for CIK 0001181412 show no filing after a Form 4/A on Sep 30. The Q3 report that would be most likely to overturn this view does not exist yet.

    The call is the same research view as v3. The wording is not. v3 used trade-instruction wording, including an entry zone. That wording is gone. Scenario figures below are model outcomes under stated assumptions. They are not instructions.

    Orbital real estate stays. v3 found that low-orbit rights are a real constraint and a lease, not a deed, and that they explain about 15% to 25% of the Starlink moat, as an assumption. Nothing filed since then changes that. The occupancy chart is not on this page, because its satellite counts come from a public catalog rather than a filing. The rights point rests on the FCC and the Outer Space Treaty, which are cited.

    The scarce unit

    The company says mass to orbit is the indicator of capacity that supports the space business and the expansion of connectivity and AI. In 2025 it launched 2,213 tonnes. The prospectus lists 1,901 tonnes of that as internal payload. In the first half of 2026, internal payloads were 908 tonnes. The metric that values the company is what a tonne in orbit earns per year, and what the next tonne will cost.

    Link to the view: the stock is not priced on today's tonnes. It is priced on a much larger future tonne.

    Unit economics, one Falcon 9, two uses

    Figures are from the Q2 earnings exhibit or the 10-Q unless marked. Dollars are millions per launch.

    Sold ride. Launch-services revenue in the first half was $978M on 17 customer launches, or $57.5M each (derived). The list price on the company sheet is $74M. Space cost of revenue was $610M over those 17 launches, $35.9M each, and that is an upper bound because the line also carries development and Dragon costs. Gross profit per sold ride is at least $21.6M (derived). Space segment gross margin was 66% in the second quarter, per the v3 reading of the filing.

    Filled with Starlink. The earnings exhibit counts 61 internal launches and 908 tonnes of internal payload in the first half, or 14.9 tonnes each. The 10-Q counts Falcon launches separately from Starship: 60 internal Falcon launches and 1 Starship in the half, against 77 Falcon launches of which 17 were for customers. The totals match. The 61 includes the Starship flight. We keep the earnings-exhibit definition and say so.

    Mass launched for internal use from 2023 through the first half of 2026 was 1,005 plus 1,418 plus 1,901 plus 908 tonnes, or 5,232 tonnes. Using that as a proxy for mass still in orbit is an assumption. Older satellites retire. Newer ones are still up. The v3 range was 4,500 to 6,000 tonnes.

    Second-quarter connectivity revenue of $4,291M, times four, is $17.2B a year. Divided by 5,232 tonnes, that is $3.28M of revenue per tonne-year (derived). A four-year life is an assumption inside the company's stated three to five years. Lifetime revenue per internal launch is about $195M (derived). Against $57.5M for a sold ride, that is 3.4x revenue. After the Q2 connectivity adjusted EBITDA margin of 60.5% (derived: $2,597M segment adjusted EBITDA divided by $4,291M), satellite capex, and the launch itself, the cash gap is smaller than the revenue gap. v3 put the cash advantage at about 2.2x to 3.2x. We did not rebuild that cash range from a new filing, because no new filing exists. It stays an estimate, labeled as one.

    The 60.5% margin is not printed. The 10-Q reconciliation shows Q2 segment adjusted EBITDA of $(205)M, $2,597M, $1,146M and $3,538M in the same column order as the operating table: Space, Connectivity, AI, Total.

    Reconciliation, tolerance plus or minus 15%. Average second-quarter subscribers of 11.15M times $66 times three months is $2,208M, against reported consumer revenue of $2,485M, a gap of 11%. Inside tolerance. Ten second-quarter customer launches at the $74M list price would be $740M, against launch-services revenue of $648M, a gap of 14%. Inside tolerance.

    ARPU fell from $85 to $66 in a year. The filings attribute that to international expansion and lower-priced plans. Internal mass launched in the first half of 2026 was 908 tonnes, against 938 tonnes a year earlier. The network is still adding subscribers. It is not adding revenue per tonne.

    Link to the view: the core earns well per tonne. The price needs far more tonnes, and far more value per tonne, than today.

    Why the words and the money disagree

    The prospectus describes an integrated space, connectivity, and AI company, a lunar presence as a step toward Mars, and a goal of putting up to 100 gigawatts of compute power into orbit a year. It sizes a $28.5T addressable market, of which $26.5T is AI. Those are company statements, not results.

    The money went somewhere else in the first half. Capex was $28,476M. AI was $23,551M, about 83%. Connectivity was $2,699M. Space was $2,226M. Nameplate compute was 1.4 GW. The orbital part is still research and development. The bridge is Starship. Without a much cheaper tonne, orbital compute does not pencil.

    They are pouring Starlink cash and IPO proceeds into terrestrial AI compute because AI is the only demand large enough to use a much cheaper tonne, and leasing compute now earns while Starship and orbital compute are unproven. If it works, it raises revenue per tonne above the Starlink figure.

    A less flattering reading, also consistent with the filings: the AI segment lost $6,355M from operations in 2025 while connectivity earned $4,423M, per the prospectus. Folding the AI lab into the launch company gave a cash-burning effort access to Starlink cash, a $25B note deal, and the IPO. A second reading: a $26.5T AI story supports a multiple that a launch and broadband company would not carry on its own. The issuer also owns the social network where that story spreads, and the 10-Q describes a Cursor collaboration to improve existing models, including the issuer's own. That is a filing fact about the business, not a claim about who wrote this note.

    Orbital real estate, kept

    Low orbit is limited by interference, drag, and the need to keep satellites from hitting each other. The limit is physics plus a rulebook. The rulebook can be rewritten. The Outer Space Treaty bars national appropriation of orbit. An FCC authorization is a license with milestones, not a deed.

    v3 measured who holds which shells, using a public catalog, and read the FCC Gen2 grant, the 2026 spectrum-sharing order, and the ITU bringing-into-use milestones. The verdict, carried forward because no newer filing overturns it: the orbital position is real, and it is mostly the launch moat expressed in orbit. A rival that cannot launch cannot occupy. A rival that can launch can file. Rights decay if they are not brought into use. We still treat about 15% to 25% of the Starlink moat as this rights layer, and that range is an assumption, not a measurement.

    The bear angles stand. The shells are less scarce than the filings make them look if the altitude bands can be tightened. The license can be capped, waived, or conditioned. A treaty bars ownership of the place itself. Concentration is a political target. None of that is a reason to mark the launch business at zero. It is a reason not to treat a filing as a title.

    The occupancy chart stays in the research pack. It is not on this page. Its counts are not SEC filings and not the company's own table.

    Link to the view: rights make the Starlink cash engine harder to copy. They do not, by themselves, justify the equity value.

    What the price requires

    Method, all assumptions. Required 2031 EBITDA equals enterprise value times 1.10 to the fifth, divided by 20. The 20x multiple and the 10% hurdle are assumptions, not facts. Enterprise value is the Oct 2 close times 13.57 billion shares, minus $60.6B of net cash. Shares are the July 28 cover counts plus the Cursor shares issued on Aug 14. Interim burn and later dilution are ignored, which flatters the price.

    The Aug 14 8-K does not print one share count. It prints 389,289,254 Class A shares for Cursor stock, plus 1,752,426 for vested restricted stock units. The sum, 391,041,680, is derived. Unvested restricted stock units (about 29.1M) and assumed options (about 44.4M) are not in the share count. Equity value at $158.96 is $2.158T (derived). Enterprise value is $2.097T (derived).

    At a 20x multiple and a 10% hurdle, that enterprise value needs about $169B of EBITDA in 2031. Trailing adjusted EBITDA is a small fraction of that. The second-quarter annualized figure is $14.2B (derived, $3,538M times four). The gap is about 12 times the run rate.

    Three operating paths, all assumptions, in billions of 2031 EBITDA. Core only: about $25B. Plan mostly works: about $72B. Vision works: about $205B. Weights we use: 40%, 45%, 15%. The price needs something close to the vision path. We give that path 15%, because it needs a Starship cadence that does not yet exist, many times more compute than 1.4 GW, and capital well beyond the cash on hand.

    A core-only reading of today's earnings, using generous assumed multiples (connectivity adjusted EBITDA at 25x, space earnings before Starship research at 20x, AI adjusted EBITDA at 20x, plus net cash), lands near $36 a share. That figure is a model, not a fact, and not an instruction. Most of the equity value is the option on Starship, AI scale-up, and orbital compute.

    Model outcomes under stated assumptions

    These are model outcomes at 3 and 12 months under the assumptions in the right-hand column. They are not instructions. Probabilities are ours. They are not frequencies. The geometric midpoint is the headline because returns compound. Share count is 13.57B, with no further dilution.

    Twelve-month geometric midpoint: $141.59. Arithmetic midpoint: $150.75. Both are model math. The geometric figure is the one we use. It sits below the last close. That is why the view says more downside than upside under these assumptions. It is not a forecast, and it is not an instruction.

    What changed versus the first Oct 4 draft, and why it still stands. The 12-month base outcome was cut from $165 to $150 in v2 because $165 needed a 2031 profit only the vision path clears, and we weight that path at 15%. The bull outcome was cut from $260 to $250, and its probability from 25% to 20%, because it needs more than that path. The bear probability rose from 30% to 35%. v3's orbital review did not move any of those figures. This pass did not either. The Q3 filing that could move them is not out. The close did not change.

    What would change this view

    The single filing most likely to overturn it is the Q3 earnings release or the Q3 10-Q. It was not on EDGAR at 18:13 ET on Oct 4. Until it is saved, the operating picture is the June quarter.

    A more constructive reading would need that filing to show AI revenue at or above $3.75B, which is one quarter of the $1.25B monthly rate in the prospectus, with the 90-day termination unused, plus two operational Starship flights that actually deploy V3 satellites. A darker reading would need a disclosed end or repricing of a named cloud contract, reported ARPU below $60, or a quarter with fewer than 30 Falcon launches and no Starship replacement.

    The prospectus already sets an Oct 9, 2026 date for up to 328.4M Class A shares, 7% of the shares under the 180-day lock-up. That supply is a fact about the calendar. It is not, by itself, a prediction of the price.

    Methods and gaps

    Share count is the July 28, 2026 cover count plus the two issued amounts in the Aug 14 8-K. The sum is labeled derived. Enterprise value subtracts cash, equivalents, and marketable securities, and adds debt and finance leases, all at June 30, 2026.

    The 3.4x figure uses first-half launch-services revenue divided by customer launches, first-half internal tonnes divided by the earnings-exhibit internal-launch count, second-quarter connectivity revenue times four divided by the mass proxy, and a four-year life. The life and the mass proxy are assumptions. The inputs are cited.

    The 2031 EBITDA figure is enterprise value times 1.10 to the fifth, divided by 20. Change the multiple or the hurdle and the required profit changes. We do not treat 20x or 10% as facts.

    Launch counts: use the earnings exhibit for "internal launches" (61 in the half, including Starship) and the 10-Q when the sentence is about Falcon only (60 internal Falcon, plus 1 Starship).

    Not in this note, on purpose. No price chart. No price file. No peer multiple built from a market-data feed. No outside price opinion is carried as ours. The Google monthly figure that appears in press is not in a filing we saved, so it does not carry a conclusion. Q3 results are unpublished. Satellite occupancy counts are one observational cluster and are not used here as a standalone conclusion.
